product.what: A web app for a job take-home: a customer-support AI agent for Paylane, a fictional fintech app (cards, transfers, refunds). The agent must follow a refund and verification policy even when customers push back, lie, or try to trick it.
screens: Playground: chat with the agent as one of 12 test customers. Next to the chat, every decision behind each reply is shown: which tools ran, whether each action was allowed or blocked and under which policy rule, and four probabilities from a classifier (fraud report, legal threat, account closure, attempt to change the rules).
Eval report: 12 scripted conversations, each run three times, with pass, fail or needs-review for every check, and the transcript behind each check.
audiences: Engineers at Fini who build AI support agents for a living. They are judging a job candidate, skim fast, and want to see why the agent did what it did.
Paylane's head of support, who is not technical and needs to understand at a glance what the agent does, what it refuses, and when it hands a customer to a person.
The candidate, demoing it live in a job interview over screen share.
product.success: Within one minute a reviewer understands the score and watches the agent refuse something, such as splitting a $180 refund into three $60 refunds, and can see exactly why.
product.must_avoid: Looking like a generic AI-generated dashboard or template.

the_record.look: A white sheet styled like a court transcript on a cool gray background. Numbered lines run down the left margin beside a thin red double rule. Speakers are labelled in capitals (CUSTOMER, AGENT). Every action the agent takes is written into the transcript as a short note in parentheses that links to an 'exhibit' card in a right-hand column. A blocked action appears in red with strikethrough, and a red 'ruling' panel names the policy rule, for example R5, over the $75 limit. The classifier's probabilities are marks on thin lines with the 0.5 hand-off threshold marked. The conversation is set in a text serif, labels in a plain sans. In the eval report, each check cites the exact transcript line numbers it is about.
the_record.risk: The courtroom framing may feel cold or adversarial for a customer-support product, and serif text reads more like a document than a chat.

authorization_slip.look: The chat sits in the middle on a white panel in a plain sans, with customer messages in light gray blocks. On the right, a dark 'printer' column holds a narrow white receipt that prints each decision the way a card terminal does: identity check APPROVED, the transaction details, automatic refund DECLINED in a red block with code R5, then REFERRAL with the hand-off ticket number. The classifier's probabilities print as small dotted bars. The receipt uses uppercase monospace type.
authorization_slip.risk: Receipts are a common fintech visual motif, and a narrow column of uppercase monospace text is harder to scan for details.

category_standard.look: A familiar software-as-a-service layout like Intercom or LangSmith: white and light-gray surfaces, the Inter font, a blue accent. The chat uses speech bubbles, blue for the customer on the right and white for the agent on the left. A right-hand 'Trace' panel lists each step as a rounded card with colored pill badges (green Verified, red Blocked R5, blue ticket TK-0001), and the classifier's probabilities are blue progress bars.
category_standard.risk: Looks like many other dashboards, including many AI-generated ones, so it may not be memorable.
